props.title: The Split
props.initialSlug: Ex-cons plot daring $3M football stadium heist

sections.content: The Split (1968) marks a crucial moment in both heist films and African American cinema. Jim Brown leads a stellar cast including Diahann Carroll and Gene Hackman in this adaptation of Richard Stark's Parker novel "The Seventh." As the first R-rated film from MGM, it pushed boundaries while delivering a gritty heist narrative. The film follows McClain (Brown) assembling a crew to rob the Los Angeles Coliseum during a packed football game - a setup that influenced later stadium heist sequences in films like Ocean's Eleven (2001) and The Dark Knight Rises (2012).

sections.content: The late 1960s marked a transformation in how Black actors were portrayed in crime films. While Sidney Poitier was breaking barriers in dramatic roles with In the Heat of the Night (1967), Jim Brown carved out a different path through action films. The Split showcases Brown's commanding screen presence while avoiding many stereotypes of the era. The complex heist planning and execution scenes established templates that influenced films like Thief (1981) and Heat (1995).

Quincy Jones' score for The Split deserves special attention, bridging orchestral film music with contemporary jazz and funk elements. This musical approach would later become a signature of Black action cinema in the 1970s, especially in films like Shaft (1971) and Super Fly (1972). The film's Los Angeles setting also provides a grittier alternative to the glossy heist films of the era like Topkapi (1964). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Heist Film

sections.content: The Split represents a crucial evolution in heist film dynamics. While earlier films like The Asphalt Jungle (1950) focused on the meticulous planning of the crime, The Split spends equal time on the aftermath and the psychological toll of betrayal. This shift influenced later films like The Killing (1956) and The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973), where the post-heist fallout becomes as important as the crime itself.
